tip: French 'has' confidence rather than being confident: 'avoir confiance en' = to trust. 'Ayez confiance en vous' = have faith in yourselves.
'-er' verbs drop the '-s' in the 'tu' command, but '-ir' verbs keep it: 'réfléchis', not 'réfléchi'.
The 'il' in 'il va pleuvoir' is a placeholder, not a person – like the 'it' in 'it's raining'. Weather verbs like 'pleuvoir' normally take no real subject.
'Asseyez-vous' – in a command, the pronoun goes after the verb with a hyphen. In the negative it moves back in front: 'ne vous asseyez pas'.
'What's wrong' is literally 'what isn't going': 'ce qui ne va pas'. The verb 'aller' (to go) doubles as 'to be OK' – 'ça va' = it's going/fine.
No question word needed – just a rising tone and a '?'. 'Tu as reçu mon message ?' is a full yes/no question, same words as the statement.
'Before' + an action needs 'de' plus the plain verb: 'avant de jouer' = before playing. French uses the plain verb where English uses the -ing form.
'Affaires' here isn't 'affairs' – it means your things or belongings. 'Rangez vos affaires' = put away your stuff.
'L'addition' here is the restaurant bill, not a maths sum. 'Je paierai l'addition' = I'll pay the bill. You ask for it with 'L'addition, s'il vous plaît'.
French has no separate '-ing' tense: 'je te parle' means both 'I talk to you' and 'I'm talking to you'. Context tells you which.
'Pouvoir' in conditional: 'tu pourrais' (you could). Very common for polite requests.
French usually uses 'the' for body parts, not 'your': 'Donne-moi la main' = give me your hand (literally 'the hand'). The owner is already obvious.
In everyday French 'on' means 'we': 'on est pressés' = we're in a hurry. It takes a singular verb ('est') even though it means us.
After 'quand' French uses the future where English uses the present: 'quand nous aurons économisé' = 'when we've saved'. Both clauses stay future.
'Chez' means 'at someone's place' in one word: 'chez des amis' = at friends' house. No English equivalent – it usually points to a person's home or shop.
French doesn't 'need' – it 'has need of': 'avoir besoin de'. 'Tu auras besoin de ton passeport' = you'll need your passport.
For an unreal 'if', 'si' takes the imperfect and the result takes the conditional: 'si tu lui parlais... il comprendrait' – never 'si' + conditional.
'Offrir' means to give as a gift, not to 'offer': 'lui offrir un livre' = to give him a book. A present is normally 'offrir', not 'donner'.
No 'à' or 'de' between 'aller' and the next verb, despite English 'going TO order': 'on va commander une pizza'.
'Je vais préparer' = 'I'm going to make': present of 'aller' + the plain verb is the everyday way to talk about the future.
'Avaient essayé' is the 'had done' past – one step further back than a past event. They had already tried several places before finding 'le bon' (the right one).
To make a command negative, 'ne' goes before the pronoun and 'pas' after the verb: 'ne vous inquiétez pas'.
The conditional softens a blunt wish: 'elle aimerait vivre' = she'd like to live, gentler than 'elle aime' or 'elle veut'.
'Valoir le coup' is literally 'to be worth the blow' – the everyday way to say something's worth it. 'Ça vaudrait le coup' = it'd be worth it.
For time still to come, 'dans' means 'in', not 'within': 'dans cinq minutes' = five minutes from now, not sometime in the next five.
'Décollera' = 'will take off': the one-word future, common for scheduled events like flights and trains.
'Finir par' + a plain verb = to end up doing something. 'Tu finiras par comprendre' = you'll end up understanding.
French weather often runs on 'faire' (to make): 'il fera sûrement très chaud' = literally 'it will surely make very hot'. Same for cold and wind – 'il fera froid'.
French drops the 'on' before weekdays: 'lundi' alone means 'on Monday'. Add 'le' – 'le lundi' – and it flips to 'on Mondays', every week.
Where English says 'when I'm done', French looks ahead: 'quand j'aurai terminé' is literally 'when I will have finished'. Future stacks on future.
